metadata.title: The OECD’s ‘Well-being 2030’ agenda: how PISA's affective turn gets lost in translation

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This article does not report an empirical student-level statistical modeling workflow using PISA microdata (e.g., no regression/ML estimation with sampling weights). Instead, it provides a qualitative critique grounded in cross-economy comparisons of PISA 2018 student feeling item translations and reported score patterns for selected emotions. Because the paper does not specify an analytic subsample, PV construction, or any complex-survey estimation procedure, there is no documented use of PISA sampling weights (e.g., student design weights) or replicate weights. For replication or quantitative follow-up, analysts would need to use the official PISA 2018 microdata and apply the PISA complex survey design weights when estimating any population-representative statistics, and to use the appropriate PV handling for cognitive achievement outcomes (though this paper focuses on affective items rather than PV-based achievement).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not conduct an empirical predictive/quantitative analysis that models PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes; it focuses on translation equivalence and interpretive critique of PISA 2018 affective items and reported score patterns across economies. As a result, Plausible Values handling is not applicable to the study’s described analytical approach. Missing-data handling is also not reported because the paper does not specify an analytic dataset construction step, missingness rule, or estimation procedure requiring imputation/deletion decisions.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper does not describe an analytic subsample drawn from PISA 2018 microdata (e.g., grade filters, item-completion thresholds, or exclusion rules). Instead, it compares reported PISA 2018 student feeling score patterns across selected economies that share the same written language (China, Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan) and contrasts them with English-language contexts (Canada, UK, USA) using published score snapshots. Therefore, no explicit sample filtering criteria for an estimation sample are provided.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 microdata the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Well-being, finding that This article is a conceptual/interpretive critique of how the OECD operationalizes the Well-being 2030 agenda through PISA 2018’s “students’ feelings” measures. Rather than training or evaluating machine-learning models, the authors compare cross-economy patterns in reported emotion-related item responses and argue that translation equivalence is not achieved even within the same written language (China, Hong Kong, Macao, Taiwan), citing differences in the Chinese terms used for emotions such as “proud,” “afraid,” and “sad.” The paper also situates these measurement issues within broader Western psychological frameworks (e.g., independent vs. interdependent self-construal) and argues that the OECD’s approach treats equivalence as a technical engineering problem. Methodologically, the study does not report sampling-weighted estimation, PV handling, missing-data procedures, or quantitative model performance metrics, limiting any causal or statistical generalization beyond the authors’ interpretive claims. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse because the manuscript does not present an empirical ML/predictive modeling study with a defined target variable, model training, validation metrics, or a documented analytic sample from PISA microdata. The authors’ “innovative analytical strategy” is qualitative/interpretive (translation comparison across economies) rather than a supervised learning pipeline, so fields required for empirical ML (e.g., ml_techniques, main_findings with performance metrics, PV handling, missing-data handling) are not populated. The paper also does not provide per-country sample sizes or an estimation sample definition, preventing extraction of total_students and n_students.
